title: Electromagnetism II
description: Electromagnetism at the advanced undergraduate level, taught partly by Alan Guth: vector analysis and index notation, the integral form of electrostatics and field energy, conductors, image charges and separation of variables, Legendre polynomials and spherical harmonics built from traceless symmetric tensors, the multipole expansion, magnetic dipoles and fields in matter, electromagnetic waves, potentials and gauges, retarded potentials and radiation.
cosmologyNeeds: The CMB power spectrum is an expansion of the sky's temperature in spherical harmonics, so the multipoles and Y_lm of this course are what the C_l of 8.286 and 8.902 are built on. Radiation from accelerated charges and the scattering of light by charges lead to Thomson scattering, which kept the early universe opaque until recombination. Index notation, the Kronecker delta, the Levi-Civita symbol and rotations of tensors are the language 8.962 (general relativity) assumes from its first lecture.
notes: The source is the course's 17 lecture-notes PDFs (no videos, no transcripts); the syllabus follows the file numbers mit8_07f12_ln1 to ln17, which match the numbering on OCW's lecture-notes and calendar pages. The notes are not one per class lecture (the course had 37): some are typed addenda by Guth (1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9), some are scanned handwritten lecture notes or slides with no text layer (3, 5, 6, 10, 11), and 14 to 16 are Guth's slides for the last three lectures; apart from Min Chen's research talk of November 21 (notes 12), OCW has no notes for the class lectures between notes 11 (Lecture 26) and notes 14 (Lecture 35). Notes 12 is a research talk by Min Chen on reversed Cherenkov radiation in metamaterials (optional, some images removed for copyright). Notes 13 is "Courtesy of Hongsheng Chen and Min Chen. Used with permission." and is not used. Notes 17 is Min Chen's final-exam review. Notes 15 has slides with a YouTube still excluded from the CC licence, and notes 16 says its diagrams are from Griffiths: draw our own diagrams. Textbook: Griffiths, Introduction to Electrodynamics, 3rd edition.
